title: Closest Values At Least X Apart
statement:
You get an integer array nums and an integer x. Choose two indexes i and j that are at least x positions apart, meaning |i − j| ≥ x. Return the smallest possible value of |nums[i] − nums[j]|.

When x = 0 you may pick the same index twice, so the answer is 0.

examples.why: 5 and 6 are the closest values overall, but they sit next to each other. The best allowed pair is 6 and 12, two positions apart.
With no distance rule, any element paired with itself gives 0.
Only the first and last elements are 3 apart: |10 − 1| = 9.

hints: Fix the right index j. Which elements is it allowed to pair with?
All elements at indexes ≤ j − x. As j moves right, that allowed set grows by exactly one element: nums[j − x]. Nothing ever leaves it.

Keep the allowed values in a sorted structure. For nums[j], the best partner is the largest allowed value ≤ it or the smallest allowed value ≥ it. A sorted set (or a Fenwick tree over compressed values) finds both in O(log n).

explain.intuition:
Fix the right end j. Its allowed partners are everything at index j − x or earlier. Move j one step right and the allowed set gains exactly one value, nums[j − x], and loses none. So you have a growing set and one question per step: which value in the set is closest to nums[j]?

In a sorted collection the closest value is always a neighbour: the predecessor (largest ≤) or the successor (smallest ≥). JavaScript has no built-in sorted set, so compress the values to ranks and keep a Fenwick tree of counts: "how many allowed values are ≤ v" plus "find the k-th smallest allowed value" give both neighbours in O(log n). In Java or C++ a TreeSet / std::set does the same in two lines.
steps: Sort the distinct values and give each a rank; build an empty Fenwick tree of counts over the ranks.
Let c = number of inserted values ≤ nums[j]. If c > 0, the c-th smallest is the predecessor; if c is less than the set size, the (c + 1)-th is the successor. Update the best difference with both.
pitfalls: Sorting the whole array and comparing neighbours. Sorting throws away the indexes, so you can't enforce the distance rule.
Inserting nums[j] itself, or nums[j − x + 1], an off-by-one that lets pairs only x − 1 apart through.
Checking only the predecessor. The closest allowed value may be larger than nums[j].

solutions.title: Check every allowed pair
solutions.idea: Try every pair of indexes at least x apart.

solutions.title: Growing sorted set via a Fenwick tree
solutions.idea: As j moves right, add nums[j − x] to a sorted structure and look up the neighbours of nums[j] in it.

followups: The distance rule becomes |i − j| ≤ x instead. What changes? (The set now also loses elements.)
Return the pair of indexes, not just the difference.
